summary:
Centre-Val de Loire stands under France's national framework. Criminal law, the custody rules of the French Criminal Procedure Code, anti-discrimination law, identity-document rules and the law on marriage apply uniformly across French regions, and no source in the inventory records a departure specific to this region.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is custodial. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents rather than lived gender. Trans women whose documents are marked male — the majority, who have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery — are therefore held in men's facilities. Each establishment then improvises its own arrangement: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers most in prison. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records an inmate told 'We don't want any women here!' alongside threats of violence, and documents the detention of Kara B., an American trans woman, in conditions Hazan describes as worrying. Accounts collected in the same feature describe heightened vulnerability to assault and to suicide under isolation.

Practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's oversight bodies record discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition the baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism and custodial-inspection authority, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

That opinion found serious and persistent violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons — placement by birth sex, isolation, exposure during strip searches — while recording no such violations in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The contrast indicates that the exposure is concentrated in the adult custodial estate rather than in care or youth settings.

The mechanism recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. It explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention, and it issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national custodial-inspection authority examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, alongside ministry and association input. That volume, sustained over a decade, indicates a persistent rather than episodic pattern of complaints.

The Défenseur des droits framework decision rests on case files and association testimony, and the 64% identity-discrimination figure it cites places France against the wider EU survey population rather than against any French region.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in France was reformed in 2016, and the terminology of that law has since changed; the CGLPL's coverage of places of deprivation of liberty now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees as well as trans detainees.

Detained trans people may route complaints to the CGLPL, which has examined roughly forty such referrals since 2010 and has issued binding guidance that places of deprivation of liberty are required to follow. That guidance addresses placement by birth sex, the isolation of vulnerable detainees, exposure during strip searches and suicide prevention.

Residents may bring cases to the Défenseur des droits, which issues framework decisions and official guidance directed at service providers on how trans people are to be treated.

Marriage between same-sex partners has been available since the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013.

Prison placement for a trans resident is decided by the gender inscribed on identity documents, with each facility improvising between special units and isolation; treatment therefore varies between establishments, and the arrangement is subject to parliamentary question and to custodial-inspection oversight rather than to a statutory rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports any inspection visit, detention case, border incident or discriminatory refusal of service located in Centre-Val de Loire itself. The CGLPL's 2021 inspections named Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, all outside this region, so regional conditions here are not sourced.

Sourcing on access to gender-affirming healthcare, on public bathroom and facility access, and on hate-crime offences recorded in this region is absent from the inventory. Whether any French hate-crime provision was applied to an incident involving a trans visitor in Centre-Val de Loire is unresolved and not sourced.

Whether Louna's placement in the Tarbes men's prison has since changed, and the outcome of oral question no. 219, are unresolved in the inventory; the sources establish only that placement remained under parliamentary scrutiny.

The date of the Défenseur des droits framework decision on trans rights is not stated in the inventory, and its operative provisions are summarised there only in general terms.

The inventory gives no figure for how many trans travellers were stopped or questioned at French entry points beyond the single account of 7 March 2017, so the frequency of document-related questioning at the border is unresolved.
